topics.title: Maxwell's prediction and the first EM waves

learn.hook: Long before Wi-Fi and 5G, a Scottish physicist doing algebra on paper predicted invisible waves that travel at the speed of light. A few decades later, they were found.
points: Faraday showed a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Maxwell asked: does a changing electric field produce a magnetic field? He concluded it does.
Maxwell's equations then predicted electromagnetic (EM) waves of linked, changing E and B fields, travelling at about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹: the speed of light. So light itself is an EM wave.
In 1887 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected EM waves in the laboratory, confirming Maxwell.
Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata produced and studied EM waves of much shorter wavelength (about 25 mm to 5 mm).
Guglielmo Marconi transmitted EM waves over many kilometres, opening the era of radio communication.

example.q: Why was Maxwell's calculated speed of EM waves such a big deal?
steps: His theory gave the wave speed as 1/√(µ₀ε₀).
This came out equal to the measured speed of light.
So light must be an electromagnetic wave.
example.answer: It showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, uniting optics with electricity and magnetism

learn.reallife: J.C. Bose's millimetre-wave work at Presidency College, Kolkata, in the 1890s anticipated technologies now used in 5G and car radar.

learn.hook: While a capacitor charges, current flows in the wires but no charge crosses the gap. Yet a compass placed near the gap still feels a magnetic field. Maxwell found the missing current.
points: Ampere's law fails while a capacitor charges: a loop around the wire gives ∮B·dl = µ₀i through a flat surface, but zero through a surface passing between the plates. The results contradict each other.
Between the plates, the electric flux ΦE changes. Maxwell defined displacement current id = ε₀ dΦE/dt.
Ampere-Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(ic + ε₀ dΦE/dt) = µ₀(ic + id).
The total current (conduction + displacement) is continuous: in the wires it is all ic, in the gap it is all id, and they are equal.
So a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.

example.q: A capacitor is being charged by a current of 2 A. What is the displacement current between its plates?
steps: Charge on plate q = ε₀EA = ε₀ΦE

learn.reallife: Electrical engineers designing high-frequency circuits for ISRO's satellites must account for displacement currents through capacitors and even through the air gaps between conductors.

topics.title: Maxwell's equations and how EM waves are made

learn.hook: Four short equations describe every electric and magnetic phenomenon, from a static zap to a 5G signal. The fourth one makes waves possible.
points: Maxwell's equations: (1) Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀; (2) Gauss's law for magnetism ∮B·dA = 0; (3) Faraday's law ∮E·dl = -dΦB/dt; (4) Ampere-Maxwell law ∮B·dl = µ₀ic + µ₀ε₀ dΦE/dt. Plus the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B).
Stationary charges make only E; charges in uniform motion (steady currents) make steady B; but accelerated charges radiate EM waves.
An oscillating charge (for example in an antenna) produces an oscillating E, which produces an oscillating B, and so on: the wave carries away energy at the charge's frequency.
In an EM wave, E and B oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel: EM waves are transverse.
E, B and the direction of propagation follow the order E × B, giving the direction the wave travels.

example.q: An electron oscillates in an antenna at 100 MHz. What frequency does the radiated wave have, and why?
steps: The fields oscillate at the same frequency as the charge.
So the wave frequency is 100 MHz.
example.answer: 100 MHz, the frequency of the oscillating charge

learn.reallife: The tall masts of Doordarshan and All India Radio have antennas in which electrons are made to oscillate; these accelerated charges launch the waves your TV or radio picks up.

topics.title: Nature and properties of EM waves

learn.hook: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to cross 150 million km of empty space, carrying enough energy to power the solar parks of Rajasthan and to push on solar sails.
points: For a wave travelling along z: Ex = E₀ sin(kz - ωt), By = B₀ sin(kz - ωt), with k = 2π/λ and ω = 2πν. E and B are in phase.
Speed in vacuum: c = ω/k = νλ = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. In a medium: v = 1/√(µε).
The amplitudes are related: E₀/B₀ = c (and E/B = c at every instant).
EM waves need no medium. They carry energy and momentum; on absorption they exert radiation pressure. Momentum delivered p = U/c for total absorption.
Example: a wave with B₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁸ T has E₀ = cB₀ = 6 V m⁻¹.

example.q: A plane EM wave of frequency 30 MHz travels in vacuum along x. At some point E = 9 ĵ V m⁻¹. Find B there.
steps: Direction: E × B must point along +x, and ĵ × k̂ = î, so B is along +z (k̂)

learn.reallife: ISRO's solar panels on satellites and India's solar parks absorb sunlight energy; the same light also delivers a tiny momentum, which spacecraft designers must account for over long missions.

topics.title: EM spectrum: radio, microwave and infrared

learn.hook: Your FM radio, the microwave oven warming leftover biryani and the TV remote are all using light that your eyes cannot see.
points: The EM spectrum is arranged by frequency or wavelength. The regions overlap; there are no sharp boundaries.
Radio waves (λ > 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in antennas. AM band 530 kHz to 1710 kHz; FM band 88 MHz to 108 MHz; TV bands from 54 MHz up to 890 MHz; mobile phones use UHF.

Microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm): produced by special vacuum tubes such as klystrons and magnetrons, and Gunn diodes. Used in radar for aircraft navigation and in microwave ovens, where they heat food by agitating water molecules.

Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): 'heat waves', given out by hot bodies and vibrating molecules. Used in TV remotes, night vision, physiotherapy heat lamps, and the greenhouse effect warms Earth by trapping IR.
Infrared is detected by thermopiles and bolometers, and many snakes can sense it.

topics.title: EM spectrum: visible, UV, X-rays and gamma rays

learn.hook: Your eyes see only a thin slice of the spectrum, from about 400 nm to 700 nm. Beyond violet lie rays that can disinfect water, image bones and treat cancer.
points: Visible light: about 700 nm (red) to 400 nm (violet). The eye is most sensitive near the middle (yellow-green). Some animals see beyond: honeybees see into the ultraviolet, and snakes can sense infrared.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): produced by the Sun and special lamps. Most solar UV is absorbed by the ozone layer. UV lamps sterilise water and instruments; precise UV lasers are used in LASIK eye surgery. Welders wear special glass goggles to protect eyes from UV.
X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): produced by bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons. Used for medical diagnosis and cancer treatment; overexposure damages tissue.
Gamma rays (below about 10⁻³ nm): produced in nuclear reactions and emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.
Higher frequency means higher photon energy, and generally more harmful to living tissue.

example.q: A radiation has wavelength 300 nm. Identify it and one use.
steps: 300 nm is shorter than violet (400 nm).
It lies in 400 nm to 1 nm.
It is ultraviolet, used to sterilise water.

learn.reallife: Water purifiers in many Indian homes use a UV lamp to kill bacteria, and cancer hospitals like Tata Memorial use high-energy X-rays and gamma rays in radiotherapy.

topics.title: EM spectrum: the full table and problem practice

learn.hook: One table summarises it all: from radio waves longer than a cricket pitch to gamma rays smaller than an atomic nucleus.
points: Radio (> 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in aerials; detected by receiver aerials.

Microwave (0.1 m to 1 mm): klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes; detected by point-contact diodes. Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): vibrating atoms and molecules; detected by thermopiles, bolometers, IR film.
Light (700 nm to 400 nm): electrons in atoms dropping to lower energy levels; detected by the eye, photocells, photographic film.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): inner shell electrons in atoms; detected by photocells and photographic film. X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): X-ray tubes or inner shell electrons; detected by photographic film, Geiger tubes, ionisation chambers.
Gamma rays (< 10⁻³ nm): radioactive decay of nuclei; detected the same way as X-rays. To identify a region, convert using c = νλ and compare with the ranges.

quiz.explain: ν = c/λ = 3 × 10⁸/5 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 6 × 10¹⁷ Hz (X-ray region).

quiz.q: Which radiation's wavelength is closest to the size of an atom (about 10⁻¹⁰ m)?
quiz.explain: 0.1 nm lies in the X-ray region.
steps: X-rays: 1 nm to 10⁻³ nm, which contains 0.1 nm

quiz.q: The displacement current between capacitor plates is 0.15 A. What is the rate of change of electric flux (in units of 10¹⁰ V m s⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I tell which part of the spectrum a wave belongs to?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Find the wavelength using c = νλ, then compare it with the ranges in the spectrum table. Sorted!
teach.nudge: Good! What formula connects frequency and wavelength, and what do you compare with?

revise.summary: Each region of the EM spectrum has its own source and detector, from aerials for radio to Geiger tubes for X-rays and gamma rays. To identify a radiation, convert with c = νλ and compare the wavelength with the ranges.
focus: Sources and detectors of each region
Identifying a region from ν or λ
remember: X-rays and gamma: film, Geiger tubes, ionisation chambers
Visible light: electron transitions in atoms
traps: Don't compare µm or nm values directly with ranges in metres; convert first
A wavelength of atomic size (~0.1 nm) is not ultraviolet; it is in the X-ray range
